content: 1. Diphenoxylate HCl and Atropine: Both agents increase sedation. Close monitoring is advised when these drugs are co-administered. Use caution and observe for signs of excessive sedation. 2. Atropine and Hyoscyamine: Both drugs reduce cholinergic effects and transmission. Caution is required, and patients should be closely monitored for potential anticholinergic side effects. 3. Atropine and Hyoscyamine Spray: Similar to the above, both agents decrease cholinergic effects. Use caution and monitor closely for any adverse reactions. 4. Atropine and Iloperidone: Atropine reduces the levels of iloperidone by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both drugs. Additionally, iloperidone enhances the effects of atropine through pharmacodynamic synergy. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 5. Diphenoxylate HCl and Iloperidone: Both drugs increase sedation. Atropine also decreases iloperidone levels via pharmacodynamic antagonism. Use caution and monitor closely for sedation and other side effects. 6. Atropine and Imipramine: Both agents reduce cholinergic effects. Diphenoxylate HCl and imipramine together increase sedation. Imipramine may also increase atropine levels through an unknown mechanism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but close monitoring is recommended. 7. Atropine and IncobotulinumtoxinA: Atropine enhances the effects of incobotulinumtoxinA through pharmacodynamic synergy. Drugs with anticholinergic effects may potentiate botulinum toxin effects, leading to excessive neuromuscular weakness and heightened systemic anticholinergic effects. Close monitoring is essential. 8. Atropine and Ipratropium: Both drugs decrease cholinergic effects. Due to the poor systemic absorption of ipratropium, interactions are unlikely at standard dosages. However, caution and close monitoring are still advised. 9. Diphenoxylate HCl and Isocarboxazid: These drugs interact through pharmacodynamic synergy, increasing the risk of toxicity. Isocarboxazid significantly increases the toxicity of diphenoxylate HCl through an unknown mechanism, with risks including hypotension, hyperpyrexia, somnolence, or even death. These drugs should not be used together, and a 14-day washout period is recommended. 10. Diphenoxylate HCl and Isoproterenol: Diphenoxylate HCl increases sedation, while isoproterenol decreases it. The clinical effect of this interaction is unclear, so caution and close monitoring are advised. 11. Ketamine and Diphenoxylate HCl: Both drugs increase sedation. Use caution and monitor closely for excessive sedation. 12. Diphenoxylate HCl and Ketotifen (Ophthalmic): Both agents increase sedation. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 13. Lasmiditan and Diphenoxylate HCl: Either drug can enhance the sedative effects of the other. Co-administration with other CNS depressants, including alcohol, has not been evaluated in clinical studies. Lasmiditan may cause sedation and other cognitive or neuropsychiatric adverse effects. Close monitoring is required. 14. Lemborexant and Diphenoxylate HCl: Both drugs increase sedation. Dosage adjustments may be necessary when lemborexant is co-administered with other CNS depressants due to potentially additive effects. Monitor closely. 15. Atropine and LetibotulinumtoxinA: Atropine enhances the effects of letibotulinumtoxinA through pharmacodynamic synergy. Drugs with anticholinergic effects may potentiate botulinum toxin effects, leading to excessive neuromuscular weakness and heightened systemic anticholinergic effects. Close monitoring is essential. 16. Diphenoxylate HCl and Levalbuterol: Diphenoxylate HCl increases sedation, while levalbuterol decreases it. The clinical effect of this interaction is unclear, so caution and close monitoring are advised. 17. Levetiracetam and Diphenoxylate HCl: Both drugs increase sedation. Use caution and monitor closely for excessive sedation. 18. Levocetirizine and Diphenoxylate HCl: Both agents increase sedation. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 19. Atropine and Levodopa: Anticholinergic agents like atropine may enhance the therapeutic effects of levodopa but can exacerbate tardive dyskinesia. At high doses, anticholinergics may reduce the effects of levodopa by delaying its gastrointestinal absorption. Close monitoring is recommended. 20. Diphenoxylate HCl and Levorphanol: Both drugs increase sedation. Use caution and monitor closely for excessive sedation.
